title: Life wasted without praise
hookLine: gun gobind gaaio nahee: if you haven't sung His praises, your life is wasted (Salok M9 1, ang 1426)

lines: THE END OF A COMPLETE READING.
cards: At the end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, after days of continuous recitation, the reader reaches the last few pages.

The family who arranged the reading is often sitting close, sometimes after a wedding, sometimes after a death. What's read near the very end is a run of short couplets by Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Salok Mahalla nine.
So these lines are heard at the turning points of Sikh family life. The first one is a single breath long, and it doesn't waste a word.

teach.b: The first salok begins gun gobind gaaio nahee, janam akaarath keen. In paraphrase: you haven't sung the praises of the Lord of the world; you've made your life useless. Gun means virtues, qualities.
Gobind is the Lord who sustains the world. Gaaio is sung. And akaarath is for nothing, to no purpose, close cousin to the akaaj of Jaijavanti.
Then the second line, in paraphrase: says Nanak, O mind, love the Lord the way a fish loves water. Stop on that fish. A fish doesn't visit the water now and then, or praise it once a week.
Water is where it breathes. Take it out, and it gasps. That's the kind of praise the salok means: not a polite compliment, but the thing you can't live without.
Notice the verb, too: sung. Sikh devotion is deeply musical. The Granth is set in ragas, kirtan fills the gurdwara, and praise here is often literally singing.
The salok doesn't call a life without praise evil.
It calls it akaarath, unused, like an instrument left in its case.
And it's addressed to the mind, man, not to someone else.
The Guru isn't scolding a crowd; he's speaking quietly to the inner voice of whoever is listening.
Sikhs commonly count fifty-seven of these saloks, and many more are coming in the days ahead: short, steady, and very honest about time. The first one sets the tone.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the very end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, at the bhog ceremony that closes it, often held for weddings, new homes and funerals.

o: a short couplet at a reading's end
a raga sung at the close of day

games.q: life wasted without praise — tap the pairs.
p: the Lord who sustains the world
how the mind should love the Lord

s: the ninth Guru's saloks are read near the end of a complete reading of the Granth
they come in the last pages, heard at the bhog ceremony.
the first salok calls a life without praise evil
it calls it akaarath, unused, like an instrument left in its case.
the salok compares the mind's love to a fish's love for water
water is where a fish breathes; it can't live without it.

games.q: the first salok wants the mind to love the Lord. what picture does it give?
o: a guest who visits on holidays.
a bird that flies far away.
games.why: says Nanak, O mind, love the Lord as a fish loves water: not a visit, but where you breathe.

practice: If you know a shabad, or even just Waheguru, sing or hum it softly now, once or several times, without worrying about your voice; if singing feels strange, hum one long note and feel it in your chest.
If you don't pray, sing a line of anything that makes you grateful, then sit and feel what's left in the body after the sound.

wordCard.voice: Gun, virtues, qualities. The first salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur says a life that never sings the Lord's gun goes unused, and asks the mind to love the Lord like a fish loves water.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gun, virtues or qualities, said with a short u as in 'put'. The salok asks us to sing the Lord's gun.

carryVoice: Your line: sing, while there's time. Like a fish in water: not a visit, a home. Day five hundred eighty-nine, sung.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1426)
